title: EV Charging Station Setup in India: 8 Things to Plan Before Installation
summary: Planning an electric vehicle charging station in India? Learn 8 practical things to check before installation, from site selection and EV charger cost to power load, DISCOM connections, safety and charging requirements.
body_markdown:
Setting up an **electric vehicle charging station** sounds straightforward.


Choose a charger. Find a parking space. Connect the power. Start charging.


In practice, there is a lot more happening between buying an **EV charger** and getting your first vehicle plugged in.


The charger itself is only one part of the setup. The site, electrical load, DISCOM connection, vehicle compatibility, safety systems, civil work, software and even the way drivers enter and leave the parking area can affect the final installation.


If you’re planning a charging station for a hotel, office, apartment, commercial property, fleet or highway location, it helps to think through these things before you order the hardware.


Here are 88 things worth planning first.


## **1. Start With the Site, Not the Charger**


This is probably the easiest mistake to make.


You see a 60 kW **DC fast charger** , decide that’s what you want, and start looking for a place to install it.


Reverse the order.


Look at the site first.


How many vehicles can actually reach the charging bays? Can a car enter, park, charge and leave without blocking another vehicle? Is the location visible from the road? Is there enough space for the electrical equipment and cable routing?


These details matter more than they initially seem.


For public charging, the Ministry of Power’s planning guidance also emphasizes accessible locations, clearly marked charging spaces and enough room for vehicle movement.


A good site should make the charging process feel simple.


Drive in. Park. Plug in. Charge. Drive out.


If drivers have to reverse through a narrow parking area while another vehicle is waiting behind them, the problem isn’t the charger.


It’s the site layout.


### **Check these before finalising a location:**


- Entry and exit access


- Parking-bay dimensions


- Vehicle circulation


- Distance from the electrical connection


- Cable-routing path


- Space for electrical panels and other equipment


- Drainage and weather exposure


- Visibility and signage


- Lighting and security


- Expected vehicle traffic


Plan the physical layout before buying equipment.


## **2. Work Out Your Charging Requirement**


Not every location needs a DC fast charger.


A workplace where cars stay parked for six or eight hours has a very different requirement from a highway site where drivers want to continue their journey quickly.


That’s where AC and DC charging start to make more sense.


An AC charger is often suited to places where vehicles remain parked for longer periods. DC charging is useful when reducing charging time is a priority.


The right choice depends on **who will use the station and how long they normally stay** .


Statiq, for example, offers[AC charging options from 7.4 kW to 22 kW](https://www.statiq.in/ac-chargers) and[DC charging solutions](https://www.statiq.in/dc-chargers) ranging from 60 kW to 360 kW for different site requirements.


The point isn’t to install the biggest charger available.


It’s to install the charger that matches the site.


Before deciding, ask:


**Who is going to charge here?**


- Apartment residents?


- Office employees?


- Hotel guests?


- Fleet vehicles?


- Highway travellers?


- Delivery vehicles?


- Multiple vehicle types?


That answer should drive your charger selection.


## **3. Check the Available Electrical Load Before You Buy Hardware**


This is one of the most important conversations to have early.


Your property may have electricity. That doesn’t automatically mean it has enough available capacity for the charging setup you’re planning.


A high-power charging installation can require additional electrical infrastructure.


The Ministry of Power’s 2024 guidelines allow EV charging station owners to apply for **Low Tension (LT) connections for loads up to 150 kW** , subject to the applicable provisions and connection process.


So before finalising your charger, check:


- Existing sanctioned load


- Proposed charging load


- Available capacity at the site


- Whether a separate connection is required


- Whether additional electrical infrastructure is needed


- Applicable DISCOM requirements


Don’t wait until the charger arrives to discover that the site’s electrical setup needs an upgrade.


That’s how an installation that looked simple starts getting expensive and delayed.


## **4. Don’t Look at the EV Charger Cost Alone**


When someone asks, *“How much does it cost to install an EV charging station?”* , the charger price is only one piece of the answer.


Your total project cost can involve:


- Charger hardware


- Electrical cabling


- Distribution equipment


- Protection equipment


- Metering


- Earthing


- Civil work


- Mounting or foundation work


- Signage and parking markings


- Internet/connectivity requirements


- Software or network integration


- Additional electrical infrastructure, where required


- Land or site costs


- Installation and commissioning


A 7.4 kW AC setup and a high-power DC charging site aren’t comparable projects.


So don’t ask only:


**“How much does the charger cost?”**


Ask:


**“What will it take to make this site ready for the charger?”**


That gives you a much more realistic picture of the investment.


## **5. Match the Charger to the Vehicles**


A charger can only be useful if the vehicles you want to serve can actually use it.


Check the charging compatibility of your target EVs before selecting the hardware.


The Indian EV charging ecosystem includes different AC and DC charging standards and connector types. NITI Aayog’s charging standards reference includes Type 2, CCS and Bharat charging standards among the recognised options.


For a commercial site, this becomes even more important.


Imagine installing a charger and discovering that the vehicles most likely to use the location have a different charging requirement.


The hardware is working.


The station is still not useful enough.


Also remember: **charger power and vehicle charging speed are not the same thing.**


A vehicle connected to a higher-powered charger doesn’t automatically charge at that charger’s maximum rated power. The vehicle’s onboard charging capability and charging system determine what it can actually accept.


## **6. Plan Electrical Safety Properly**


An EV charging station is an electrical installation handling substantial power. The installation needs appropriate protection, wiring, earthing and other safety provisions based on the equipment and applicable electrical standards.


The Ministry of Power’s guidelines require EV charging infrastructure to comply with applicable technical, safety and performance requirements. India also has BIS standards covering EV charging infrastructure and related safety requirements.


Depending on the installation, the electrical design can involve equipment such as:


- MCBs or suitable circuit protection


- RCD/RCCB protection where applicable


- Earthing


- Surge protection


- Isolators


- Properly rated cables


- Distribution panels


- Protective enclosures


Don’t simply ask an installer to “connect the charger.”


Ask for the electrical design.


You want to know what is protecting the charger, the vehicle and the people using the station.


## **7. Think About Weather, Drainage and Physical Protection**


A charger sitting outdoors deals with more than electricity.


It deals with rain, dust, heat, accidental impacts and everyday vehicle movement.


Look closely at the location.


Does rainwater collect there?


Could a vehicle hit the charger while parking?


Is the equipment exposed to unnecessary sunlight or water?


Can cables become a trip hazard?


Would a bollard or other physical protection help protect the equipment?


These details often disappear from the conversation when everyone is focused on charger specifications.


They shouldn’t.


For example, Statiq’s current hardware range includes outdoor-oriented equipment with specified protection ratings such as IP66 for its Nectar AC charger and IP55/IK10 for its DC charging hardware.


The exact protection requirement still depends on the product and installation environment.


The site should suit the charger—not the other way around.


## **8. Plan the Digital Side Before Going Live**


A modern charging station isn’t only a physical machine.


There is a software layer behind it.


Drivers increasingly expect to see things like:


- Charger availability


- Charging status


- Pricing


- Location


- Payment options


- Session information


- Fault or availability updates


The Ministry of Power’s 2024 guidelines encourage open communication protocols such as **OCPP, OCPI and UEI** to support connected and interoperable charging infrastructure


This is particularly relevant for public charging.


You don’t want a charger installed perfectly but invisible to the people trying to find it.


Statiq combines its charging hardware with a[charging management system](https://www.statiq.in/ev-charging-software/csms) and driver app, allowing operators to manage chargers while users can locate and use connected charging infrastructure.


Think about the digital experience before commissioning the station.


## **A Practical Pre-Installation Checklist**


Before you place the equipment order, run through this list.


### **Site**


- Land or parking rights are clear


- Entry and exit are practical


- Charging bays have enough space


- Vehicle movement has been considered


- Drainage and weather exposure have been checked


### **Electrical**


- Existing sanctioned load is known


- Required charging load is calculated


- DISCOM requirements are confirmed


- Metering requirements are understood


- Electrical protection and earthing are planned


### **Charger**


- AC/DC requirement is clear


- Vehicle compatibility is checked


- Required charging power is identified


- Charger specifications match the site


- Applicable standards/certifications are verified


### **Operations**


- Pricing model is decided


- Payment method is planned


- Software/network connectivity is ready


- Maintenance responsibility is clear


- Charger monitoring is available


### **Customer experience**


- Charging bays are clearly marked


- Signage is visible


- Lighting is adequate


- Users can find the station


- Entry and exit are straightforward


## **The Part People Usually Underestimate**


Installing the charger is only one milestone.


Getting the site ready is the real project.


A good **electric vehicle charging station** starts with the location, then the electrical requirement, then the charger, and finally the customer experience.


Get those decisions in the right order and the installation becomes much easier to manage.


Choose the hardware first and try to make the site fit around it, and you’ll probably spend more time—and potentially more money—fixing problems that could have been avoided.


**Plan the site. Check the power. Match the charger. Build for the people who will actually use it.**


That’s a much better starting point for EV charging infrastructure in India.


## **FAQs**


**1. Can anyone set up an electric vehicle charging station in India?**


The Ministry of Power’s 2024 guidelines designate setting up and operating EV charging stations as a de-licensed activity. The operator still needs to comply with the applicable technical, safety, electricity and other requirements


**2. Is a DC fast charger necessary?**


Not always.


If vehicles remain parked for several hours, AC charging may be sufficient. If the location is designed around shorter charging stops, DC fast charging can make more sense.


Start with the usage pattern.


**3. How much does an EV charger cost?**


There isn’t a single standard price. Charger cost depends on factors such as charger type, power rating, configuration and manufacturer. The overall installation cost also includes site-specific electrical and civil work.


**4. Can an EV charging station be installed at a hotel, office or apartment?**


EV charging infrastructure can be deployed in private, semi-restricted and public locations, including office buildings, educational institutions, hospitals, group housing societies, commercial properties and public locations, subject to the applicable requirements.
